rows.en:
...Hello, everyone. Nice to meet you.
My name is Shoji Arai, from Class 2-B.
This may surprise you all, but I was in the soccer club, you know.
Back in my first year.
I quit after a year, though.
I suppose it just wasn't for me.
The practices were hard, and even to be generous, my athletic ability was nothing to speak of.
But you see, the real reason was something else.
Did you know this school has a fully equipped dormitory?
Surprisingly few people know about it.
There's the auditorium, isn't there?
The auditorium where they hold graduation and other ceremonies.
Have you ever been up above that auditorium?
I don't suppose you have.
It's normally off-limits.
And hardly anyone ever uses it.
Apparently plenty of people spend three years at this school and graduate without ever knowing what's up there.
But you see, a certain few know it well.
They know there's a dormitory up there.{p}

It can sleep about fifty people.
The athletic clubs use it when a tournament is coming up, or when they hold a training camp at school.
But apparently it's really only a few of the athletic clubs that use it.
And do you know why? ...Things appear in that dormitory.
Why would that be, I wonder?
I have no idea why they'd appear in a place like that.
But the rumors about that place don't stop at one or two.{p}
When it comes to scary stories, what kind interests you most?
Ghost stories
Strange stories
Cruel stories
Disgusting stories

...I see.
So you like strange stories.
As it happens, I think the story I'm about to tell is perfect for someone like you.
I think you'll be satisfied.
...Yes.
After all, even I, who actually lived through it, still don't really understand it.
...It happened during summer vacation last year.{p}

You know the soccer club is split into a first team and a second team, don't you?
And the second-team players, which is to say people like us, were made to hold a training camp at school.
Of course, our treatment and our standing were different from the first team's core players, the regulars included.
First-team players don't stay overnight at school.
We hardly ever even got to see them.
However you looked at it, we had neither the talent nor the grit to move up to the first team.
If anything, rather than getting stronger or winning tournaments, I'd have been happy just to have fun in club activities.
But according to the first-team people, that makes you a loser.
The second team is a bunch of losers like that.
Players get dropped from the first team to the second, but almost nobody ever moves up from the second to the first.
But for me, that actually made it easier.
So what if you're a loser, as long as you're having fun?{p}
You think so too, don't you, {a}?
Being a loser is fine by me
I don't want to be a loser
I don't care either way

...I see.
So you're not the same kind of person as me, {a}.{p}

In this world, you see, there are people who rule and people who are ruled.
You're the ruling type, aren't you?
Me, I find it more comfortable being ruled.
...I see.
So that's the kind of person you are, {a}.
...Well, never mind.
Let's go on with the story.{p}

I liked the soccer club, that bunch of losers, because it was easygoing, but some people in it didn't feel that way.
Our soccer club is fairly strong, after all.
It was a far cry from the fun club activities I'd pictured.
The practices were hard, and everyone was serious.
But you see, plenty of people felt the same way I did.
People who wanted a friendlier, more relaxed soccer club, even if it meant being weak.
And so I found a friend I got along with.
A first-year who, like me, hated the harsh practices.{p}

His name was Masaru Sodeyama.
He had a weak constitution.
Apparently his mother told him he had to, so he reluctantly joined an athletic club.
He figured the soccer club had lots of members, so he'd be able to slack off.
Pretty much the same as me, right?
But once he actually joined, it was nothing like that, and he was depressed.
We became friends right away.
By then, we were already the soccer club's dropouts.
We could have quit any time.
But Sodeyama was a good guy.
He said his mother would be sad if he quit the soccer club, so he kept at it without missing a single one of those hellish, grueling practices.
Frankly, I wanted to quit, but Sodeyama was there.
So I kept him company and kept at it too.{p}

Besides, they say that if you were in an athletic club as a student, it goes over well in job interviews, don't they?
So I kept at it, too.
And then came the summer training camp.
I don't much like training camps.
Being forced to live a regimented life as a group, controlled twenty-four hours a day.
I think that sort of thing is unforgivable.
And it went on for a whole week.
If Sodeyama hadn't been there, I'd have skipped the camp and just quit the soccer club.
I'm no good at living in a group...
When the camp starts, the first thing they do is show you to the dormitory, and you pick your own bed.{p}

My first sight of the dormitory left a thoroughly gloomy impression.
As for windows, there were only small skylights you could barely get your head through, if that, and not one bit of sunlight came in.
It was like a prison, damp and clammy, with soulless bunk beds lined up in a grid like a go board.
That was all.
They call it a dormitory, but there are only beds.
The beds were metal-pipe frames with no reading lamps, and the mattresses were thin and rock-hard.
It was like sleeping on bare tatami.
Frankly, it felt less like a dormitory than an internment camp.
Even so, there were guys who were thrilled about the camp.
Everyone eating together, everyone sleeping together.
Some people's hearts leap at that kind of group life.
Not that I can understand it.
"I got this bed!"
"This one's mine!"
They all shouted things like that, fighting over the beds they wanted.
I'd have thought every bed was the same.
"Arai, where should we go?"
Sodeyama asked me that.
If we could, it'd be better to be next to each other, right?
Sodeyama was the only one there I thought I'd get along with.
When I looked, almost all the beds were already taken.
Even if we wanted to choose, the only spot with two empty beds side by side was...{p}

"...Looks like it's only here."
With that, Sodeyama tossed his bag up onto the top bunk of a bed far from the entrance.
The bed to its right was empty.
"Then I'll take this one."
I put my things on the bed to the right of the one Sodeyama had chosen.
"...Hey, that guy picked bed number 4."
"...Yeah.
What an idiot."
I didn't miss the two guys whispering to each other nearby.{p}

Bed number 4?
I looked carefully at the edge of the bed frame.
My bed was marked with the number "2."
Sodeyama didn't seem to have noticed what those two were saying.
When I quietly peeked at his bed...{p}

His bed was marked with the number "4."
That was when I first realized it.
That Sodeyama was drawing a great deal of attention.
Everyone was putting their things away and pretending not to look, yet they kept glancing at Sodeyama, or rather, it seemed to be bed number 4 they were worried about.

I wavered over whether to tell Sodeyama about it.
Should I tell him?
Or else...{p}What do you think I did?
You told him
You didn't tell him

From that day on, the grueling practices began.
But after dinner we had free time, so we could relax.
Everyone had brought handheld video game consoles or portable CD players.
The ones who hadn't brought manga or novels, or cards and games, and everyone passed the time in their own way on their beds.
Sodeyama and I talked about all sorts of things, our studies and our hobbies.
Good times always fly by.{p}

Sodeyama was rubbing his sleepy eyes, and he looked somehow haggard.
"Looks like you didn't sleep very well."
When I said that, he gave a little nod.
"You seemed to be having nightmares..."
"...I don't really remember."
He answered wearily.
That was when I noticed.{p}

That there was a small blue bruise on the back of his right hand.
"Where'd you get that bruise?
Did you bump it on something?"
"...Huh, I don't know.
I don't really remember."
He answered as if I were bothering him.{p}

That night, too, Sodeyama seemed to sleep badly.
The next morning, his color was even worse.{p}

And the bruise on his hand had grown bigger than the day before.
It was a bruise that looked painful just to see, as if something heavy had been pressing on it for a long time, or as if someone had pinched it as hard as they could.{p}

"...Sodeyama.
Are you all right?"
"..............Yeah."
"Doesn't the bruise on your hand hurt? It looks worse than yesterday."
"..............Yeah."
He said very little.{p}

Days like that went on for a while.
And day by day, Sodeyama's health and color got worse.
He looked like someone you couldn't tell was alive or dead.
And along with it, the bruise on his right hand grew bigger too, stamping its mark ever more clearly, a dark, murky black.{p}

And at practice on the last day, he finally collapsed.
"The bed... take me to the bed..."
That was all he kept muttering.
It was hot, after all.
We thought it might be sunstroke, so it was decided to let him rest in bed.
It was summer vacation, so the school nurse wasn't there either.
"Arai, you go with him."
One of the upperclassmen told me that, and I took Sodeyama back.
Not that anyone needed to tell me; I'd meant to volunteer for the job anyway.{p}

At that point, I agonized over whether it was really all right to lay him in bed number 4.
Everyone's distant looks, like they wanted nothing to do with it.
And what those two had said to each other.
I remembered it clearly, you see.{p}{a}, what do you think I did then?
Put him in bed number 4
Put him in a different bed

I meant to do that, too.
Not bed number 4; I thought I'd at least let him sleep in my bed.
...But it was no use.
He didn't want to.
For some reason, he wanted to sleep in bed number 4.{p}

Having no choice, I laid him in bed number 4.
"...Hurry up and get out.
...I'm sleepy."
It was a really cold reception.
He chased me off as if I were in his way.
I left the room, leaving Sodeyama there alone.{p}

That damp dormitory where no sunlight came in even in the daytime.
Naturally, the stale air there turns dusty and musty.
I didn't want to stay there long either, if I could help it.
...But little by little, I started to worry.
If anything happened to Sodeyama, I'd be the one held responsible.{p}What would you do?
Go back and check on him
Keep on practicing

I see.
...You really are a cold person, aren't you?
I suppose that's how people on the ruling side are.
You can abandon a friend without a second thought.
You have that kind of face, after all.
But I was different.
Friends are important, you know.{p}I was worried about Sodeyama, so I went back to the room.{p}
...Sodeyama was asleep.
He was lying on the bed with the blanket pulled up over his head, and it was squirming.{p}

...But what I'd taken for a blanket was a living thing.
An unknowable creature like a caterpillar, its whole body wrapped in a pale brown, blanket-like cloth, was lying over Sodeyama.
"Ah!"
I cried out before I could stop myself.
The instant I did, the thing stopped moving.{p}
Then it slowly looked my way.

Below the neck it was wrapped tightly in that blanket-like rag, so I couldn't see its whole body.
Not that I wanted to see it, of course.
It had an indescribably horrible face.
You could almost call it a woman's face, but that thing was definitely not human.
It didn't seem like a ghost or anything of that sort either; it was simply an eerie monster.
It had a hand in its mouth.
Sodeyama's right hand.
A shock, as if time had stopped.
All around me, a silent world without a single sound.
If someone had dropped a needle right then, I think I could have heard even that.
And then, in that silent world, what did I hear but a slurp, slurp, like something sipping, like something sucking.
It was sucking on Sodeyama's arm.
On that dark, murky bruise, its lips pursed, it was sucking away.{p}

Then all of a sudden, it opened its mouth wide.
It was a mouth so huge it looked like it could swallow a human head in one gulp.
...I couldn't run away.
Strangely, I even forgot to run.
Fear left me unable to move, and that tangled together with the shock of meeting something unknown; my five senses were stolen from me.
It kept glaring at me, its huge mouth still wide open.{p}I couldn't run away. What do you think I did?
You screamed
You prayed
You spat at it
I don't know
You know, I don't know myself what came over me, but I spat.{p}
Right at that monster.{p}

Then all of a sudden, it let out a shrill shriek like fingernails scraping glass, and began to writhe in agony.
Where my spit had hit it, it sizzled and charred and smoke rose up, as if I'd thrown sulfuric acid on it.
I was stunned.
It melted into the air just like that and vanished.{p}

Whether it died or ran away... that I can't tell you.
Only once it was gone did I hurriedly grab Sodeyama's arm, which hung limply out from under the covers.

"Sodeyama!"
I pulled as hard as I could.
And then I froze in horror.
Sodeyama wasn't there.{p}

What came out from under the covers was only Sodeyama's right arm.
The rest of Sodeyama, the body that should have been past the base of the shoulder, was gone.
...No, to be precise, that's not quite right.
Stuck to the base of the shoulder was something like a plant bulb.
A small thing, small enough to sit in the palm of your hand.
That was Sodeyama.
Wrinkled, shriveled and hardened, it was all that was left of Sodeyama.
It was almost strange that only his right arm was still normal.
Had all the nourishment been sucked out of Sodeyama's body?
And if I'd found him just a little later, would the nourishment in the last thing remaining, his right arm, have been sucked out too, leaving only a wrinkled lump?{p}

Even if I told anyone what happened to Sodeyama, there was no way they'd believe me.
So I kept quiet.
But even if I kept quiet, Sodeyama had disappeared, that was a fact, and I was the one who'd been with him until the end, so I figured I'd be questioned.
But nothing happened.
The moment it came out that Sodeyama had been sleeping in bed number 4, I was called in by the principal.{p}

Even though it was summer vacation, the principal came all the way to school.
And then,
"You saw nothing.
Nothing happened there.
Is that clear?"
he told me, making very sure I understood.{p}

I don't know how that incident was dealt with.
But I never saw Sodeyama again after that, and he didn't come to school even when the second term started.
And I don't know what became of that shriveled thing that was all that was left of Sodeyama, either.
...That's the direct reason I quit the soccer club.
...By the way, after that, I heard the rumor about bed number 4 secondhand.
Apparently, anyone who uses bed number 4 goes missing.
But whenever someone tries to get rid of that bed, something bad happens, so no one dares lay a hand on it.
Still, what was that monster I saw?
Does the principal know something?
A while later, I read in a certain book that some monsters of folklore are weak against human spit.
Maybe that thing was one of them.
But I don't believe it died.
If it were the kind of thing that would disappear that easily, someone would have gotten rid of it long ago.
{a}, the day may come when you have to use the dormitory, too.
When it does, check whether bed number 4 is still there.
I'm sure it will be.
But I'm warning you, be very careful.
Don't use bed number 4...
This concludes my story.
Next person, please.{p}
